# Draft:A Monument to Mariano Fortuny

The Monument to Mariano Fortuny () is a sculptural monument at the corner of Carrer del Pintor Fortuny and Carer d'en Xuclà, on the rear facade of the former Tabacos de Filipinas Building, in El Raval, Barcelona. Created by Miquel and Llucià Oslé in 1922 and inaugurated in 1942, it is dedicated to the Catalan painter Mariano Fortuny (1838–1874).
History
The idea for a monument to Fortuny arose in 1911, under the leadership of the city councillor Ignasi Iglésias. A commission was formed the following year to launch the project, but it did not advance. In 1918 the proposal was revived by the Cercle Artístic de Sant Lluc and the art critic Joaquim Ciervo, and a campaign of lectures, exhibitions, newspaper articles, and fundraising was organized to promote it. The work was commissioned from the Oslé brothers, and the City Council of Barcelona was asked to provide a site for the monument; early suggestions included Royal Square and the gardens in front of Virreina Palace.
The sculptors began work, but the failure of the Bank of Barcelona, where the money for the monument had been deposited, brought the project to a halt. In 1932 the initiative was revived again, this time led by the City Council. Carrer del Pintor Fortuny was chosen because it already bore the painter's name, and because the fire that had destroyed the El Siglo department store had made it possible to extend the street through to La Rambla. Because the street was relatively narrow, a niche had to be opened for the statue, which had originally been conceived as a freestanding sculpture; it therefore lost its rear view, which critics had considered especially successful in its treatment of drapery. The outbreak of the Spanish Civil War in 1936 again delayed installation. After the end of the war, an article in La Vanguardia by Carles Fages de Climent belatedly recalled the centenary of Fortuny's birth and emphasized the neglect of the monument. The City Council resumed the project, and the monument was finally inaugurated on 20 June 1942.
Description
The monument presentss the painter as a full-length seated figure dressed in a tunic like a Roman patrician, emphasizing the classicism of the representation. According to Lino Cabezas, although it was created at a time when the avant-garde was flourishing in Europe, the figure appears more characteristic of the 19th century than of its own period and reflects the academic training of its authors. The pose is fully classical, with one leg advanced in contrapposto, creating a counterbalanced rhythm between the legs and arms. For the face, the sculptors relied on photographs and on Fortuny's death mask, although the final result is idealized and departs from the mask's realism. The body is likewise idealized, slender and muscular like that of a classical athlete. Fortuny's profession is indicated only by the paintbrushes he holds in his left hand. Cabezas also highlights the treatment of the folds of the drapery, a feature rooted entirely in classical models.
